dersimelagon.summary: An investigational oral pill that switches on the MC1R pigment receptor to darken skin; tanning-focused circles follow it, though it was developed for light-sensitivity disorders.

quick.overview:
Dersimelagon (MT-7117) is an experimental pill that activates MC1R, the receptor that tells skin to make dark pigment. Tanning-focused circles follow it because it does what melanocortin tanning peptides do, but by mouth: more melanin, darker-looking skin.

It works by raising eumelanin, the dark pigment, in the skin. It was developed to protect people with erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) and X-linked protoporphyria from painful reactions to visible light, and it has also been studied in diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Skin darkening is an expected effect of the drug, and no study has looked at it as a cosmetic tan.
quick.how: It is a clinical-trial drug, not a consumer product. In studies it is taken as a daily pill under medical supervision by people with light-sensitivity disorders. Tanning users who follow it are interested in it as an oral alternative to injectable melanocortin peptides, and any cosmetic use is outside what it was developed for.
quick.risks: Reviewers describe its safety and effectiveness as still needing further characterization. Because it acts on the pigment pathway, skin darkening is built in. It is investigational, with no approved product or cosmetic status, so anything sold outside trials is unregulated.

angle.text: Tanning-focused circles follow dersimelagon because this oral MC1R agonist boosts skin melanin, the same route melanocortin tanning peptides take toward a darker, tanned look. It was developed for light-sensitivity disorders, and no trials have looked at cosmetic tanning.

semax.summary: A Russian ACTH-derived nootropic peptide used in study-maxxing circles for focus and learning; it is not an appearance compound, and human trials are small stroke studies.

quick.overview:
Semax is a seven-amino-acid peptide derived from a fragment of ACTH. People in looksmax and study-maxxing communities use it for focus, learning and mental sharpness rather than for how they look, and some forum posters mention libido as a side benefit.

It was developed in Russia, where it is used for stroke and other neurological conditions. Published work includes small, mostly Russian-language clinical studies in stroke and optic nerve disease, plus animal and cell studies in which it raised brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and altered gene expression after experimental stroke. No study has examined it for appearance.
quick.how: Forum users typically describe it as a nasal spray used for study or work sessions, sometimes stacked with other nootropics. Reported effects vary widely between users, from clear focus to nothing noticeable.
quick.risks: Long-term safety data are limited outside Russia, and reviews of therapeutic peptides note the lack of clinical trials. It is not approved by the FDA or EMA, and forum users often buy it from unregulated sources. Some people asking about it online are teenagers, for whom the lack of safety data matters most.

angle.text: Semax is used in study-maxxing and nootropic circles for sharper focus, learning and neuroprotection rather than for appearance, with forum posters occasionally mentioning libido. Human trials are small Russian stroke studies, and no appearance effect has been studied.

hydroxypinacolone-retinoate.summary: HPR, sold as Granactive Retinoid, is a gentler cosmetic retinoid used for fine lines, dark spots and breakouts by people who find retinol irritating.

quick.overview:
Hydroxypinacolone retinoate (HPR) is a retinoic acid ester used in over-the-counter skincare, best known as Granactive Retinoid. People use it for fine lines, dark spots and acne with less irritation than retinol or tretinoin.

Retinoids speed up skin turnover and support collagen, which smooths texture and evens tone. HPR is described as binding retinoid receptors directly rather than needing conversion, which is the explanation given for its lower irritation. Small Italian studies tested HPR gels in acne and Chinese studies tested it in anti-aging serums, mostly in combination formulas.
quick.how: It is applied as a serum or cream, usually in the evening, and is often chosen by people whose skin does not tolerate retinol. It is commonly paired with a moisturizer and daytime sunscreen. Visible changes in texture and tone generally take weeks to months of regular use.
quick.risks: Trials of HPR-containing products report mild dryness, peeling, redness and burning, in about 15% of participants in one open study. A laboratory study found retinoid products often lose potency with light and storage. Pregnancy safety data for HPR were not found, and retinoids in general are usually avoided during pregnancy.

angle.text: HPR, sold as Granactive Retinoid, is a gentler cosmetic retinoid: it acts on skin cells to speed turnover and support collagen, so fine lines soften and dark spots even out. People who find retinol irritating often choose it, and published human studies are small and mostly use combination products.

retinaldehyde-retinal.summary: The vitamin A form one step before retinoic acid, sold in over-the-counter serums as a middle-ground retinoid for wrinkles and uneven tone.

quick.overview:
Retinaldehyde (retinal) is a form of vitamin A that sits one step from retinoic acid, the active retinoid in prescription tretinoin. In skincare it is sold over the counter as a step between retinol and tretinoin, for smoother skin, fewer wrinkles and more even tone.

Skin converts retinal into retinoic acid, which acts on retinoid receptors to change cell turnover and gene expression, and supports collagen. Skin-specific studies are few: an exploratory 1999 trial in facial rosacea, a 1999 human tolerance study, and a registered split-face study of 56 people with aging skin.
quick.how: People apply it as a serum or cream, usually at night, and often alternate it with stronger prescription retinoids while skin adjusts. Results in texture and tone build over weeks to months, with sunscreen used by day.
quick.risks: No published data in the sources quantify irritation for retinal on skin, though retinoids in general can cause dryness, redness and peeling. Retinal is chemically reactive and oxidizes readily, so product stability matters. Retinoids are generally avoided in pregnancy.

angle.text: Retinal is an over-the-counter retinoid that skin converts into retinoic acid, which speeds cell turnover and supports collagen for smoother, more even skin. It is used as a middle step between retinol and prescription tretinoin, and skin-specific human studies are few.

trifarotene-aklief.summary: Aklief is a prescription retinoid cream approved in 2019 for acne on the face and trunk, backed by large vehicle-controlled trials.

quick.overview:
Trifarotene (Aklief) is a prescription topical retinoid from Galderma, approved by the FDA in October 2019 for acne in people aged 9 and older. It is used for clearer skin on the face, chest and back, and users discuss it as a step between tretinoin and isotretinoin.

It selectively activates retinoic acid receptor gamma, the most common receptor type in skin. Like other topical retinoids it normalizes skin-cell turnover, which clears clogged pores and calms breakouts. Its pivotal trials enrolled people with acne on both face and trunk, giving it rigorous truncal data other topical retinoids lack, and later phase 4 trials have looked at post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and acne scars.
quick.how: It is a once-daily cream applied in the evening to affected areas, prescribed by a clinician and used alongside a moisturizer and sunscreen. Acne improvement is judged over weeks to months of consistent use. It carries an acne approval only, not an anti-aging one.
quick.risks: The most common reactions are application-site irritation, itching and sunburn. The label advises moisturizer, reduced frequency if needed, and sun protection. Trial data have not identified a pregnancy-related risk, but case reports with other topical retinoids describe birth defects like those from oral retinoids. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Aklief is a prescription retinoid cream that selectively activates RAR-gamma to clear pores and calm breakouts, giving clearer skin on the face, chest and back. It is FDA-approved for acne and tested in large vehicle-controlled trials; it carries no anti-aging approval.

retinyl-palmitate.summary: A storage-form vitamin A ester in moisturisers and sunscreens that gives mild retinoid action for fine lines; the gentlest and least-studied cosmetic retinoid.

quick.overview:
Retinyl palmitate is the ester of retinol (vitamin A) with palmitic acid, found in over-the-counter moisturisers, sunscreens, fortified foods and supplements. In skincare people use it as the mildest retinoid, for gradual smoothing of fine lines and tone.

Skin is thought to convert it stepwise to retinol and then retinoic acid, which acts on retinoid receptors. Reviews place it among the first-generation cosmetic retinoids with retinol and retinaldehyde; one review concluded these are efficacious, safe and well tolerated, while another notes cosmetics need no clinical efficacy studies and that retinoids face instability and low penetration.
quick.how: It is used in leave-on moisturisers and day creams, often by people wanting retinoid action with little irritation. Because it is weaker than retinol or tretinoin, any change in lines tends to be gradual.
quick.risks: A US National Toxicology Program mouse study reported faster tumour development when retinyl palmitate was applied with simulated sunlight. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel judged it safe in cosmetics up to 3% and a European committee found no phototoxic potential, so the debate over sun-exposed skin has not produced a human-use limit. High-dose supplement trials such as CARET gave it with beta-carotene to smokers and asbestos-exposed workers, and the injectable medical form carries overdose and anaphylaxis warnings.

angle.text: Retinyl palmitate is the vitamin A ester in many moisturisers and sunscreens: skin converts it to retinol and then retinoic acid for mild retinoid action and gradual smoothing of fine lines. It is the least-studied cosmetic retinoid for wrinkles, and its use on sun-exposed skin has been debated for years.

poly-l-lactic-acid-sculptra.summary: Sculptra is an injectable PLLA collagen stimulator that rebuilds cheek and midface volume gradually, with effects lasting up to about two years in trials.

quick.overview:
Sculptra is a Galderma injectable of poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA), used to restore cheek and midface volume, soften cheek lines and rebuild a gaunt face after weight loss. Results build gradually over weeks, giving fuller cheeks, softer folds and better-defined contours.

Unlike hyaluronic acid fillers, which add volume immediately, PLLA microparticles prompt a mild inflammatory response that leads the body to lay down its own collagen. The FDA first approved it in 2004 for facial fat loss in people with HIV, and later for nasolabial folds and cheek wrinkles. Systematic reviews of randomized trials report better skin elasticity, wrinkle reduction and facial volume, with effects sustained up to about 25 months.
quick.how: It is injected by trained clinicians, typically over several sessions spaced weeks apart, with volume building between visits. Looksmax forum discussion is limited to a few questions about regaining volume in a gaunt face after weight loss.
quick.risks: Reported adverse events are mostly mild to moderate: bruising, hematoma, tenderness, swelling and nodules. A 2026 systematic review reported at least one serious case. Lumps are linked to technique and product selection, which is why it is administered by clinicians.

angle.text: Sculptra is injected to bring volume back to the cheeks and midface, softening cheek lines and rebuilding a gaunt face after weight loss. PLLA triggers the body's own collagen production, so the result builds over weeks, and randomized trials report effects lasting up to about two years.

deoxycholic-acid-kybella.summary: Kybella is an injectable approved for double chins that dissolves fat cells under the chin for a sharper chin-neck line without surgery.

quick.overview:
Deoxycholic acid is a bile acid the body makes to digest fat. A synthetic version, sold as Kybella (Belkyra elsewhere), is injected under the chin to destroy fat cells and reduce a double chin, sharpening the jaw and neck line. The FDA approved it in April 2015 for adults with moderate to severe submental fullness.

Injected into fat under the skin, it acts like a detergent that disrupts fat-cell membranes so the cells burst, and the body clears the debris over several months. People discuss it as a lower-downtime alternative to liposuction for the chin and neck, and some ask about other small fat pads; the label does not recommend use outside the chin area, and off-label areas such as jowls and flanks have been tested only in small studies.
quick.how: It is a clinic procedure done in a series of injection sessions spaced weeks apart. The treated area swells for a period afterward, and the fat reduction becomes visible once swelling settles.
quick.risks: The label lists swelling, bruising, pain, numbness, redness and hardness as the most common reactions. Warnings include injury to the facial nerve branch controlling the lower lip, trouble swallowing and hair loss in the treated area. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Kybella is injected under the chin to destroy fat cells, shrinking submental fullness for a sharper chin-neck line without surgery. The fat reduction shows once swelling settles, and some users ask about other small fat pads, which the label does not cover.

polymethyl-methacrylate-pmma-filler.summary: Permanent filler beads (Artefill, Bellafill) that add lasting volume to cheeks and chin or lift acne scars; removal can be difficult.

quick.overview:
PMMA filler is made of tiny plastic microspheres in a carrier gel, sold in the US as Artefill and Bellafill. It is injected for permanent volume in the cheeks and chin and to lift acne scars, so the result is visible straight away and stays.

The microspheres are not absorbed, so the body forms fibrous collagen tissue around them, which adds lasting volume. The FDA lists non-absorbable fillers as approved only for nasolabial folds and cheek acne scars. PMMA is also the polymer in bone cement and dentures, and some bodybuilders have reportedly injected it for muscle shaping. Published cosmetic outcome data are limited to registered studies and reviews.
quick.how: It is placed by a clinician, usually in small amounts in stages. Looksmax forums mostly mention it in cautionary threads, for example when a surgeon offered PMMA bone cement for facial implants.
quick.risks: The FDA lists lumps, granulomas, infection, migration, permanent hard nodules and rare vascular injury including blindness as filler complications, some appearing years later. It says removal of permanent fillers can be difficult or impossible. Use in the buttocks, muscles or other unapproved sites is not sanctioned.

angle.text: PMMA filler (Artefill, Bellafill) places permanent microspheres in the cheeks, chin or acne scars, and the body builds collagen around them, so volume shows right away and stays. Published outcome data are limited, and bodybuilders have also injected PMMA-type products for muscle size.

poly-d-l-lactic-acid-pdlla.summary: A collagen-stimulating injectable related to PLLA, used for firmer, smoother skin, wrinkles and scar texture, with results building over weeks.

quick.overview:
PDLLA is a dissolvable polymer injected into the skin so it makes new collagen rather than just plumping one spot. It is used for wrinkles, nasolabial folds, acne scar texture and overall skin quality, and sits with PLLA and calcium hydroxylapatite in the biostimulator category.

As the particles break down into lactic acid, the body mounts a mild inflammatory response and fibroblasts lay down collagen over weeks to months, giving firmer, smoother skin over time. Published support consists of a few randomised and open-label trials plus reviews, including one comparing a PDLLA product (AestheFill) with hyaluronic acid in nasolabial folds. Forum discussion appears minimal.
quick.how: It is injected by clinicians, commonly over several sessions, with improvements building gradually between visits rather than appearing at once.
quick.risks: Reviews highlight granuloma formation and non-inflammatory nodules, which may need treatment such as triamcinolone. As with other fillers, the FDA notes some complications appear long after injection and that rare vascular events can occur.

angle.text: PDLLA is a collagen-stimulating injectable, related to PLLA, used for skin quality, wrinkles and acne scar texture: mild inflammation prompts new collagen, so skin looks firmer and smoother over weeks. A handful of trials exist, and nodules are the main known risk.

collagen-filler.summary: The original injectable filler, used to plump lines, folds and lips with visible results right away; temporary, and now largely replaced by hyaluronic acid.

quick.overview:
Collagen fillers are injected into the skin to smooth wrinkles and fold lines and to add lip volume, with the plumping visible right after treatment. Bovine collagen (Zyderm, Zyplast) was the leading filler in the US for about two decades and was long treated as the gold standard.

The injected collagen physically adds volume under a line or fold and is gradually absorbed, so the effect is temporary. Hyaluronic acid fillers have since taken over in many markets, a shift that included a randomised trial comparing Restylane with bovine Zyplast in nasolabial folds. Forum mentions of collagen today mostly concern supplements.
quick.how: It is injected by clinicians into lines, folds or lips, with repeat treatments needed to maintain the look. Fillers containing bovine collagen involve an allergy screening step beforehand.
quick.risks: Reviews note hypersensitivity reactions with bovine collagen, and the FDA advises allergy screening for fillers containing collagen. As with all fillers, bruising, swelling and lumps can occur, and results are temporary.

angle.text: Collagen filler is the original injectable, used to soften wrinkles and fold lines and to add lip volume, with the plumping visible right after treatment. It is temporary, bovine versions can provoke allergies, and hyaluronic acid has largely replaced it.

polyacrylamide-gel.summary: A permanent synthetic gel filler used for facial contouring and HIV-related facial fat loss; volume shows once placed, and removal can be difficult.

quick.overview:
Polyacrylamide gel is a water-rich synthetic gel injected as a permanent filler for facial contouring, such as cheeks or chin, and for HIV-related facial fat loss. The volume is visible once it is placed and stays, since the gel is not absorbed.

The gel works as a non-absorbable bulking material in the treated area. The same type of material is used in medicine for urinary incontinence and has been tested for knee osteoarthritis in a Danish trial. Published studies of its cosmetic use are few in the sources reviewed, so how it performs as a face filler is not well documented.
quick.how: It is injected by a clinician into the area being contoured. Because it is permanent, it is placed once rather than topped up on a schedule.
quick.risks: Polyacrylamide itself is described as low in toxicity, but the acrylamide monomer is a neurotoxin and carcinogen, and residual monomer contamination is a stated concern. The FDA says permanent fillers can cause nodules, migration and late complications, and can be difficult or impossible to remove. Registered work follows women who had polyacrylamide hydrogel removed from the breast.

angle.text: Polyacrylamide gel is a permanent injectable used for facial contouring and for HIV-related facial fat loss; the volume is visible once it is placed. Published cosmetic evidence is thin in the sources reviewed, and removal can be difficult.

mercury-skin-lightening.summary: Mercury-salt creams and soaps that pale skin by blocking melanin; banned in many countries but still found in informal markets, with serious toxicity.

quick.overview:
Some skin-lightening creams and soaps contain mercury salts, which pale skin and fade dark spots by suppressing melanin. They have a long history, from ancient Greece and Rome to 19th-century cosmetics, and are still sold in informal and online markets despite bans in many countries.

Inorganic mercury inhibits melanin production and accumulates in the skin, which can also discolour it over time. There are no clinical trials of mercury as a cosmetic treatment, and the literature is about its toxicity. It is not a treatment used in clinical dermatology.
quick.how: Products are applied to the face or body as creams, lotions or soaps over weeks to months. Some contain mercury that is not listed on the label, so buyers may not know it is present.
quick.risks: The WHO describes these products as hazardous. Kidney damage, tremor, insomnia, memory loss and headaches have been reported. A 2023 Minamata Convention amendment bars manufacture, import and export of mercury-added cosmetics after 2025.

angle.text: Mercury-containing creams and soaps are used in informal markets to pale skin and fade dark spots, because mercury salts block melanin production. They are banned in many countries, the WHO describes them as hazardous, and they have no clinical cosmetic use.

clobetasol-propionate.summary: A super-potent prescription steroid cream that turns up undeclared in illicit lightening creams, where skin paling is a side effect; documented skin harms are significant.

quick.overview:
Clobetasol propionate is the strongest class of topical corticosteroid, prescribed for psoriasis, eczema, lichen conditions and similar. It also appears as a hidden ingredient in illicit skin-lightening creams, where skin paling in the treated area is a side effect of its action.

It activates glucocorticoid receptors in the skin, dampening inflammation and suppressing pigment. The FDA has not approved it for lightening, and products containing it are sold internationally and online, sometimes at higher strength than prescription versions. A 2016 study cited in the sources ranks it with mercury and hydroquinone among the most toxic and most-used lightening agents. No trials have tested it for lightening.
quick.how: In prescription use it is a short-course cream or ointment applied to affected skin. In lightening products it is used undeclared inside creams, so people may apply it for long periods without knowing.
quick.risks: Reported effects include skin thinning, bruising, visible capillaries, stretch marks, acne, raised blood pressure and blood sugar, and adrenal suppression; Cushing's syndrome has been reported. The US label limits use to two weeks and 50 g per week, and it is prescription-only.

angle.text: Clobetasol is a prescription steroid for psoriasis and eczema that appears as a hidden ingredient in illicit lightening creams, where it suppresses pigment and paler skin follows. Use for lightening is off-label and unstudied, and its documented skin harms are significant.

decapeptide-12.summary: A cosmetic brightening peptide for dark spots and uneven tone, studied in small open-label trials inside multi-product routines.

quick.overview:
Decapeptide-12 is a ten-amino-acid peptide sold in cosmetic brightening products for dark spots, melasma and sun-related pigmentation, with users comparing it to hydroquinone. The payoff people want is fading spots and a brighter, more even tone.

It is described as inhibiting tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin, and has been reported to reduce melanin content. A 2021 pharmaceutics paper described efficacy of more than 50% over 16 weeks of twice-daily treatment, limited by poor skin penetration because the peptide is large and water-soluble. Small open-label studies report improvement in melasma scores and photodamage grades, using a 0.01% cream inside a routine that included glycolic acid and sunscreen, with no control group.
quick.how: It is applied as a serum or cream, typically twice a day, as part of a routine with an antioxidant cleanser, an exfoliating acid and daily sunscreen. Studies ran for weeks to months.
quick.risks: The open-label studies reported good tolerability and no adverse events in the small groups tested. Long-term safety data and independent controlled trials were not found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Decapeptide-12 is a cosmetic peptide marketed for brightening: it is described as slowing melanin production so dark spots fade and tone looks more even. Evidence consists of small, uncontrolled studies, often on multi-ingredient products, and skin penetration is a known limit.

rice-water.summary: Starchy rice-rinse water from Asian folk beauty, used as a hair rinse and skin wash for shine, softness and glow.

quick.overview:
Rice water is the milky liquid left over when rice is rinsed, soaked or boiled, used in parts of Asia as a hair rinse and skin wash, with fermented versions popular on social media. Proponents say it makes hair shinier, stronger and less prone to breakage, and that it soothes and brightens skin for a more even-looking complexion.

It carries starch plus small amounts of vitamins, minerals and amino acids. Proponents point to compounds such as inositol and ferulic acid as the reason it might smooth hair strands, reduce friction and support skin. A 2023 review of topical hair remedies popular on TikTok examined claims like these, and an encyclopedic overview describes studies of rice water itself as limited, with growth claims resting largely on accounts such as those of Yao women in China. No clinical trial of rice water for hair or skin appears in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: People soak or boil rice, strain off the liquid, sometimes ferment it for a day or two, then use it as a rinse after shampooing or as a face wash or toner. Users usually repeat it as part of a regular routine.
quick.risks: Topical use is generally treated as low risk, but no controlled safety data exist. Rice can contain arsenic, which is discussed mainly for drinking rice water, and prepared rice water can spoil if stored for long.

angle.text: Rice water is a folk beauty rinse from parts of Asia, used on hair for shine and less breakage and as a skin wash for softness and an even-looking complexion. It is popular in beauty communities, and no trials have tested it for hair or skin.

turmeric-topical.summary: Traditional South Asian turmeric paste and masks used for brightening skin tone and fading blemishes; it stains skin yellow.

quick.overview:
Topical turmeric means applying turmeric root or its pigment curcumin to the skin, usually as a paste, mask or cream. It is a long-standing South Asian household remedy, promoted in appearance communities for brightening, evening skin tone and fading blemishes.

Curcumin has been studied for anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and anti-proliferative activity, which is the usual rationale given for use on skin. Human research is thin: one randomised, double-blind pilot trial tested a turmeric cream in vitiligo (reported in 2022), and other curcumin trials cover unrelated conditions. No trial of cosmetic skin lightening in healthy skin was found.
quick.how: People mix turmeric powder into a paste with a liquid such as milk or yogurt, or use ready-made creams, and leave it on briefly as a mask. It is commonly used as a regular routine step.
quick.risks: Turmeric stains skin and fabric yellow. Yellow discolouration has been reported with oral supplements. Controlled safety data for topical cosmetic use are lacking.

angle.text: Turmeric pastes and masks are a long-standing South Asian preparation, used to calm and fade blemishes for a brighter, more even tone. One small vitiligo trial exists, none address cosmetic lightening, and the pigment can stain skin.

powdered-pearl.summary: Ground pearl used in Chinese medicine for about two thousand years for a luminous complexion, as a mask or taken by mouth.

quick.overview:
Powdered pearl is finely ground pearl or mother-of-pearl, a traditional Chinese medicine ingredient used for over two thousand years in beauty and health preparations. People use it for a luminous, brighter, even-looking complexion and as an anti-aging ingredient, either as a topical mask or as an oral powder.

Pearl is mostly calcium carbonate with a protein matrix. Researchers attribute antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and tissue-repair activity mainly to the water-soluble matrix proteins, studied in cells and animals. Modern research mostly covers wound healing and bone repair, with a few small human studies on other outcomes, and no trial tests it for complexion.
quick.how: It is mixed into face masks or pastes, or taken as a powder in traditional preparations, as part of a regular beauty routine. Traditional use measures results over weeks of repeated use.
quick.risks: Reviews say direct evidence on long-term safety, heavy-metal content and immune effects is limited. No safety data specific to cosmetic use appear in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Powdered pearl has about two thousand years of use in Chinese medicine for a luminous, brighter complexion, applied as a mask or taken by mouth. Research covers wound and bone repair, and its skin-brightening use rests on tradition.

trenbolone.summary: A potent veterinary-origin steroid used by bodybuilders for muscle mass and a dry, hard, vascular look; reviews of users report adverse effects in most.

quick.overview:
Trenbolone (tren) is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid used in cattle as a growth promoter. It has never been approved for human use, but bodybuilders and some looksmaxxers use it for muscle mass, strength and a lean, dry, vascular physique.

It binds the androgen receptor strongly, reportedly more so than testosterone, and is not converted to oestrogen, which is why users associate it with less water retention. Anabolic effects in muscle are inferred from animal work and user reports. No controlled human trial of its effect on muscle or appearance was found; published human research is mostly reviews of adverse effects. Some very young forum users claim it aids bone growth or height, and no studies support that.
quick.how: Users generally run it in structured cycles alongside heavy training and a diet aimed at gaining muscle or cutting fat, usually stacked with other steroids. Products come from unregulated sources, and contaminated products have been reported.
quick.risks: A 2024 review reports adverse effects in about 90 percent of users, including acne, gynaecomastia, hypertension, arrhythmia, psychiatric effects and injection-site damage. It is a controlled substance in the US and prohibited in sport.

angle.text: Trenbolone is a veterinary steroid that bodybuilders use for muscle mass, strength and a lean, hard look by strongly activating the androgen receptor. Forum posters also claim effects on height and facial structure; no human trials exist, and reviews of users report adverse effects in most.

nandrolone.summary: An injectable steroid (Deca) used by lifters for muscle size and joint comfort; trials show lean-mass gains in sick patients, none in healthy lifters.

quick.overview:
Nandrolone is an injectable anabolic steroid, best known as nandrolone decanoate (Deca-Durabolin). It has been prescribed for wasting, anaemia of kidney disease and osteoporosis, and bodybuilders use it for a bigger, fuller physique, with users also citing joint comfort and, in looksmax posts, hair-friendliness and bone growth.

It activates the androgen receptor and, unlike testosterone, is converted to a weaker androgen (DHN) rather than DHT; it also has progestogenic activity. Clinical trials in patients have examined lean mass, bone and blood outcomes and show effects on lean mass. No controlled trial in healthy people for appearance was found, and the bone-growth claim is untested.
quick.how: Lifters generally use it in cycles with heavy training, commonly alongside testosterone, since it suppresses natural production. Supply for non-medical use is illicit, and a systematic review describes illicit use as widespread among adolescents and bodybuilders.
quick.risks: Reviews of illicit use report adverse effects across several organ systems, and cardiac deaths have been reported in anabolic steroid users generally. It suppresses natural testosterone production, is a US Schedule III drug, and is prohibited in sport.

angle.text: Nandrolone (Deca) is an injectable steroid used by lifters for muscle size and, per forum claims, joint comfort and bone growth, through anabolic signalling in muscle. Trials show lean-mass gains in patients with illness, and none exist in healthy lifters.
